contract.note: Checking 'rarely tell you' against Anthropic and the wire reports is a reasonable plain reading, since that is where the figures come from. It may still be narrower than Marcus's 'boosters', who use the acronym itself; the contract flags this.

evidence.note: Company disclosure from May 2026, inside the target period. It labels the figure as run-rate revenue, so the core holds. It is also explicit about the meaning, which cuts against 'rarely tell you'.
Reuters, Aug 2026, inside the period. Calls the figure a run rate and defines it as extrapolating current sales. Supports the core, and it also clearly states the meaning.
Bloomberg summary, Aug 2026. Plainly calls the figure an annualized rate. That contradicts 'rarely tell you' for major press, though it fits the core claim.
Feb 2026 company disclosure, before the target period. Shows Anthropic has used the run-rate label consistently.

reviews.rationale: Mixed. The core holds: Anthropic's mid-2026 headline figures were run-rate revenue (e1, e2, e3). The secondary element fails on the contract's test: Anthropic, Reuters and Bloomberg all said clearly that the figures were run rate or annualized (e1–e3). Informal booster uses of 'ARR' were not sampled.

Aug 20 2026, before the post. AT&T was shifting workloads away from Anthropic to open models for cost reductions.
AP, July 2026. Tokenmaxxing was hitting its limits amid cost backlash. Weaker than 'collapse' but consistent with the claim.

reviews.rationale: Supported. Reports dated before the post show AT&T increasingly moving AI work to open models, partly away from Anthropic, explicitly to save costs (e1, e2). AP describes tokenmaxxing fading amid a cost backlash (e3). 'Collapse' overstates the reporting a little, and the evidence for other companies is thinner, but the core observation holds.
